voice_brief: Ammar. Egyptian man, mid-to-late 30s, a childhood friend back from years in Rome — confident, fast-talking, warm on the surface, a gold tooth you can practically hear. Italian polish over a Cairene base; charming even when he's lying, never raises his voice to make a point.
text: You want revenge? Get in line behind everyone else you burned on the way up. I'm not even near the front of it.

speaker: ammar
voice_brief: Ammar. Egyptian man, mid-to-late 30s, a childhood friend back from years in Rome — confident, fast-talking, warm on the surface, a gold tooth you can practically hear. Italian polish over a Cairene base; charming even when he's lying, never raises his voice to make a point.
text: Look at you. Clean hands and a full ledger. I genuinely didn't think you had it in you, habibi. I mean that as a compliment, for once.

speaker: ammar
voice_brief: Ammar. Egyptian man, mid-to-late 30s, a childhood friend back from years in Rome — confident, fast-talking, warm on the surface, a gold tooth you can practically hear. Italian polish over a Cairene base; charming even when he's lying, never raises his voice to make a point.
text: Fine. You win this one honestly, which is more than I can say for myself. Take what you came for.

speaker: ammar
voice_brief: Ammar. Egyptian man, mid-to-late 30s, a childhood friend back from years in Rome — confident, fast-talking, warm on the surface, a gold tooth you can practically hear. Italian polish over a Cairene base; charming even when he's lying, never raises his voice to make a point.
text: So we're the same now, you and I. Funny — I always thought you'd be the one left standing on principle. Guess not.

speaker: ammar
voice_brief: Ammar. Egyptian man, mid-to-late 30s, a childhood friend back from years in Rome — confident, fast-talking, warm on the surface, a gold tooth you can practically hear. Italian polish over a Cairene base; charming even when he's lying, never raises his voice to make a point.
text: Don't lecture me. You signed the same shortcuts I did. We just got caught at different times.

speaker: farid-nassar
voice_brief: Farid Nassar. Egyptian man, late fifties, measured, warm, a manager who has seen every act in Cairo.
text: The carpet merchant from Giza. Sit, sit. We open at nine; until then the room is mine and the chairs are yours. What can the Alhambra do for you?

speaker: farid-nassar
voice_brief: Farid Nassar. Egyptian man, late fifties, measured, warm, a manager who has seen every act in Cairo.
text: Whoever the Ezbekiyya wants. Some nights a name that fills the street, most nights our own singer, who is better than half the names. Take a table and you will hear for yourself. The men at the tables buy carpets too, by the way. Rich ones.

speaker: farid-nassar
voice_brief: Farid Nassar. Egyptian man, late fifties, measured, warm, a manager who has seen every act in Cairo.
text: The stairs to the gallery. Three hundred pairs of feet a night, and the runner is worn to the string. Bring me something Fine that will take it, and I pay you half again over what it is worth. The Alhambra does not haggle with its suppliers.

speaker: farid-nassar
voice_brief: Farid Nassar. Egyptian man, late fifties, measured, warm, a manager who has seen every act in Cairo.
text: Let me see it on the step. Yes. Yes, that will take the feet. Here is your money, and my thanks.

speaker: farid-nassar
voice_brief: Farid Nassar. Egyptian man, late fifties, measured, warm, a manager who has seen every act in Cairo.
text: Wearing like iron. The manager of the Kursaal asked me where it came from. I told him Giza, and to expect a queue.

speaker: nadia-wahba
voice_brief: Nadia Wahba. Syrian-Egyptian woman, early forties, composed, dry, a singer's voice used sparingly.
text: You look at my floor the way I look at a bad tenor. Good. I bought this hall with a singer's savings and a dealer's eye; the floor is what is left to fix. Sit. Tell me what you have.

speaker: nadia-wahba
voice_brief: Nadia Wahba. Syrian-Egyptian woman, early forties, composed, dry, a singer's voice used sparingly.
text: Forty tables, a company of four, and a crescent I paid a coppersmith too much for. The Pera crowd comes on Thursdays; the effendis come every night and argue about cotton. The building is sound. What it lacks is capital, and carpets.

speaker: nadia-wahba
voice_brief: Nadia Wahba. Syrian-Egyptian woman, early forties, composed, dry, a singer's voice used sparingly.
text: Something with colour for the front of the stage, where the lamps fall. Fine at least; the audience is close enough to count the knots. I pay above the market, and I remember who was useful.

speaker: nadia-wahba
voice_brief: Nadia Wahba. Syrian-Egyptian woman, early forties, composed, dry, a singer's voice used sparingly.
text: Unroll it under the lamp. Ah. That is a stage now. Take your money; the singer will thank you tonight from the middle of it.

speaker: nadia-wahba
voice_brief: Nadia Wahba. Syrian-Egyptian woman, early forties, composed, dry, a singer's voice used sparingly.
text: I said I lacked capital. Twenty-five pounds buys a quarter share of the Qamar: a little of the door every week, a word with anyone who sits at my tables, and the floor becomes your business as much as mine. I do not offer this twice a season.

speaker: nadia-wahba
voice_brief: Nadia Wahba. Syrian-Egyptian woman, early forties, composed, dry, a singer's voice used sparingly.
text: Partner. The boards in the middle of the room have been bare since the Khedive. Bring me an Exceptional rug for the centre and the house pays for it, handsomely, out of the door money.

speaker: youssef-hanna
voice_brief: Youssef Hanna. Egyptian man, sixties, patient, learned, a gentle joke under every sentence.
text: A merchant who comes before the doors open is either very keen or very lost. The hall is for listening, you understand; we do not sell anything but the silence between the songs. How can I help you?

speaker: youssef-hanna
voice_brief: Youssef Hanna. Egyptian man, sixties, patient, learned, a gentle joke under every sentence.
text: We announced a young woman from the Delta for July, Umm Kulthum; her father brings her, and she sings as though the hall were a mosque. Otherwise the conservatoire sends us its best, and the gardens send us their moths. Take a table. Nobody talks during the singing, so you will have to sell in the interval.

speaker: youssef-hanna
voice_brief: Youssef Hanna. Egyptian man, sixties, patient, learned, a gentle joke under every sentence.
text: The foyer, where they wait. Something quiet and well made; the audience should walk on it and forget it. Fine or better, and I pay a premium for restraint, which is rarer than gold thread.

speaker: youssef-hanna
voice_brief: Youssef Hanna. Egyptian man, sixties, patient, learned, a gentle joke under every sentence.
text: Lay it by the door. Nobody will notice it, which is exactly the point. Thank you. Your money, and a seat whenever you want one.

speaker: youssef-hanna
voice_brief: Youssef Hanna. Egyptian man, sixties, patient, learned, a gentle joke under every sentence.
text: Nobody has noticed it. A professor from the university stood on it for ten minutes discussing Ibn Khaldun and never looked down. Perfect.

speaker: salma-farid
voice_brief: Salma Farid. Egyptian woman, early thirties, quick, practical, cheerful, always halfway to the next task.
text: Mind the paint. Madame Nour wants the sala open and perfect and I have three days and two hands. You are the carpet man from Giza? Good. Walk with me and talk fast.

speaker: salma-farid
voice_brief: Salma Farid. Egyptian woman, early thirties, quick, practical, cheerful, always halfway to the next task.
text: Singing and short plays. Madame sings herself some nights, and we have two actors who can make a pasha laugh at his own cook. Dancers? Next year, perhaps. This year we fill the room with a song.

speaker: salma-farid
voice_brief: Salma Farid. Egyptian woman, early thirties, quick, practical, cheerful, always halfway to the next task.
text: The foyer. Everyone who matters in Cairo will stand on it on the first night and look down before they look up. Exceptional, nothing less, and Madame pays double for it. She says a carpet is the first thing a critic sees and the last thing he forgives.

speaker: salma-farid
voice_brief: Salma Farid. Egyptian woman, early thirties, quick, practical, cheerful, always halfway to the next task.
text: Unroll it, quickly, before she comes down. Oh. Oh, that is the one. Here, the money is counted; she counted it twice. Thank you. Now go before I find you a ladder.

speaker: salma-farid
voice_brief: Salma Farid. Egyptian woman, early thirties, quick, practical, cheerful, always halfway to the next task.
text: Full house, two encores, and a critic from the morning paper who stood on your carpet and wrote that the sala had taste. Madame cut it out and pinned it in the office.

speaker: kemal-arslan
voice_brief: Kemal Arslan. Turkish man, forty, poised, amused, speaks like a man counting a bar of music.
text: A carpet merchant, in the Nightingale, before the band has tuned. Orlov would like you; he likes anyone who sells something at night. I am Kemal; the band is mine, the bookings are half mine. What are you selling?

speaker: kemal-arslan
voice_brief: Kemal Arslan. Turkish man, forty, poised, amused, speaks like a man counting a bar of music.
text: Foxtrots for the diplomats, a tango for the Russians, and after midnight whatever the clarinet feels like. The dance floor is the show. Take a table; the people at the next one have money from three countries.

speaker: kemal-arslan
voice_brief: Kemal Arslan. Turkish man, forty, poised, amused, speaks like a man counting a bar of music.
text: The bar end, where the floor stops and the drinking starts. Something geometric, Fine or better, that looks well under a globe lamp at two in the morning. The club pays in good money and does not ask twice.

speaker: kemal-arslan
voice_brief: Kemal Arslan. Turkish man, forty, poised, amused, speaks like a man counting a bar of music.
text: Roll it out by the rail. Yes. Orlov will say it is too good for the bar and then stand on it all night. Your money, merchant.

speaker: kemal-arslan
voice_brief: Kemal Arslan. Turkish man, forty, poised, amused, speaks like a man counting a bar of music.
text: A Romanian countess spilled champagne on it the first night and Orlov nearly threw her out. It has survived worse since. Come and hear the band.

speaker: kassab
voice_brief: Smooth Cairene dealer, late thirties, oily charm, a little mocking, quick
text: Neighbour! Such a pleasure. Your father and I were almost friends, you know. Almost. Come, see my rugs. New, bright, cheap. Everything the tourists want.

speaker: kassab
voice_brief: Smooth Cairene dealer, late thirties, oily charm, a little mocking, quick
text: Did I say that? People hear what they want. Of course, a son would know if his father's rugs were real. Would he not? Perhaps take one to an expert. Perhaps in Damascus.

speaker: kassab
voice_brief: Smooth Cairene dealer, late thirties, oily charm, a little mocking, quick
text: Big enough, yes. For a while. Customers are like pigeons, my friend. They go where the grain is.

speaker: kassab
voice_brief: Smooth Cairene dealer, late thirties, oily charm, a little mocking, quick
text: Your customers? They have legs. They walk. If they walk to me, what can I do? Offer them tea and let them go? I am not a monk.

speaker: kassab
voice_brief: Smooth Cairene dealer, late thirties, oily charm, a little mocking, quick
text: Ha! I like you. We will see who is still here at the end of the month.

speaker: abuhamid
voice_brief: Bilgin. Young Turkish coffee-house owner settled in Giza, once a chess champion in Istanbul: calm, hospitable, well connected, enjoys his own jokes.
text: Sit, sit. You look like a man who sold something today, or a man who wants to. Coffee?

speaker: abuhamid
voice_brief: Bilgin. Young Turkish coffee-house owner settled in Giza, once a chess champion in Istanbul: calm, hospitable, well connected, enjoys his own jokes.
text: In Istanbul, once. I won more than I lost, and I lost to the right people. Now I play in the back corner for tea, or for a few piastres if you are brave. Come and sit when you have time.

speaker: abuhamid
voice_brief: Bilgin. Young Turkish coffee-house owner settled in Giza, once a chess champion in Istanbul: calm, hospitable, well connected, enjoys his own jokes.
text: A Frenchwoman came asking for "a rug with a real past". The hotel man Yusuf complains about porters. And the police moved the tourist donkeys again. Nothing changes except the prices.

speaker: abuhamid
voice_brief: Bilgin. Young Turkish coffee-house owner settled in Giza, once a chess champion in Istanbul: calm, hospitable, well connected, enjoys his own jokes.
text: Go where they are woven, habibi. The women of Fayoum sell their reed rugs for almost nothing. And at Saqqara the diggers sell old things. Some of them are even old.

speaker: abuhamid
voice_brief: Bilgin. Young Turkish coffee-house owner settled in Giza, once a chess champion in Istanbul: calm, hospitable, well connected, enjoys his own jokes.
text: Southwest, past Saqqara. A day and a half on a donkey, or take the train from Cairo. Ask for Umm Salah. Tell her Bilgin sent you and she will charge you double.

speaker: abuhamid
voice_brief: Bilgin. Young Turkish coffee-house owner settled in Giza, once a chess champion in Istanbul: calm, hospitable, well connected, enjoys his own jokes.
text: North is the Delta and Alexandria. East past Suez is Sinai: monks, Bedouin, and men who charge a toll for the privilege of not robbing you. Past that, Palestine and Syria. Take the train where there is one. Camels are romantic only in books.

speaker: abuhamid
voice_brief: Bilgin. Young Turkish coffee-house owner settled in Giza, once a chess champion in Istanbul: calm, hospitable, well connected, enjoys his own jokes.
text: Village lads from Saqqara and Fayoum will walk with you for a few piastres, and run at the first shot. Real guards you find in Cairo and Alexandria. Bedouin riders at the Tarabin camp, if Salim likes you. And out-of-work gendarmes wander the Delta roads looking for a caravan to join. Feed them well. Hungry men go home.

speaker: abuhamid
voice_brief: Bilgin. Young Turkish coffee-house owner settled in Giza, once a chess champion in Istanbul: calm, hospitable, well connected, enjoys his own jokes.
text: Whoever is thirsty that week. Carry a little money you do not mind losing, and speak politely. Most of them would rather talk than fight.

speaker: mansour
voice_brief: Sheikh Mansour. Village elder, deep, measured, dry humour, Upper Egyptian accent.
text: You are the rug man from Giza. My nephew says your cat bit him. He deserved it. What do you want in Saqqara?

speaker: mansour
voice_brief: Sheikh Mansour. Village elder, deep, measured, dry humour, Upper Egyptian accent.
text: Old? Some are old. Some were old last Tuesday. A man in the village takes new silk, soaks it in tea and sells it to Englishmen as "Pharaoh's carpet". Pharaoh did not have carpets. Buy from me what I tell you the truth about.

speaker: mansour
voice_brief: Sheikh Mansour. Village elder, deep, measured, dry humour, Upper Egyptian accent.
text: I have a silk rug like the one you keep in your corner. A widow in Helwan sold it. No papers. Maybe Damascus, maybe Kayseri. The price reflects my ignorance. Look in the market.

speaker: mansour
voice_brief: Sheikh Mansour. Village elder, deep, measured, dry humour, Upper Egyptian accent.
text: Tombs, pots, a cat mummy every week. The inspectors take everything with writing on it. Last month an Englishman paid for a whole camel of broken pottery. God is generous.

speaker: ummsalah
voice_brief: Umm Salah. Middle-aged village woman, quick, sharp, laughs easily, strong rural accent.
text: A Giza man! You people buy our rugs for nine piastres and sell them for eighty. Sit down, I want to see your face while you lie to me.

speaker: ummsalah
voice_brief: Umm Salah. Middle-aged village woman, quick, sharp, laughs easily, strong rural accent.
text: Fairly. Hm. Buy from my looms and I will sell you the good ones, not the ones the goats slept on. Look in the market.

speaker: ummsalah
voice_brief: Umm Salah. Middle-aged village woman, quick, sharp, laughs easily, strong rural accent.
text: Ground loom, pegged in the courtyard. The green is from the reeds by the canal, the blue is indigo from Cairo, and the rest is patience. A rug a week if the children let me.

speaker: ummsalah
voice_brief: Umm Salah. Middle-aged village woman, quick, sharp, laughs easily, strong rural accent.
text: Tell them anything true. Tell them Umm Salah sends her greetings and that the rug will outlive them both.

speaker: ummsalah
voice_brief: Umm Salah. Middle-aged village woman, quick, sharp, laughs easily, strong rural accent.
text: My son Salah works at the telegraph office in Cairo. His wife is expecting. Take him this rug from my loom. Do not sell it, do not let your cat sleep on it. He will give you something for your trouble.

speaker: ummsalah
voice_brief: Umm Salah. Middle-aged village woman, quick, sharp, laughs easily, strong rural accent.
text: He got it? Good. You are more honest than you look. From now on my rugs are cheaper for you. Tell nobody.

speaker: rashid
voice_brief: Uncle Rashid. Old Cairo merchant, sixties, gruff, teasing, secretly fond, fast talker.
text: You came all the way to the Wikala? Your father only came when he owed me money. Do you owe me money?

speaker: rashid
voice_brief: Uncle Rashid. Old Cairo merchant, sixties, gruff, teasing, secretly fond, fast talker.
text: Here I have the whole stock, not the three pieces I send to your corner. Buy here and you pay less, because there is no donkey to feed between us.

speaker: rashid
voice_brief: Uncle Rashid. Old Cairo merchant, sixties, gruff, teasing, secretly fond, fast talker.
text: He was a better talker than a merchant. He could sell sand to a Bedouin and then give the money to the Bedouin's daughter for her wedding. That old Fayoum rug was the last thing he bought before he stopped working. He paid too much for it and he still will not tell me why. Ask him, he changes the subject.

speaker: rashid
voice_brief: Uncle Rashid. Old Cairo merchant, sixties, gruff, teasing, secretly fond, fast talker.
text: In Damascus there is a man called Farid al-Khatib. He knows every workshop from Aleppo to Kayseri. If anyone can tell you what that rug really is, he can. It will cost you the journey and a bruise to your pride.

speaker: rashid
voice_brief: Uncle Rashid. Old Cairo merchant, sixties, gruff, teasing, secretly fond, fast talker.
text: Old families in Heliopolis and Zamalek, and Hagop the Armenian in the Khan, who buys anything for resale. He pays little, but he pays today.

speaker: hagop
voice_brief: Hagop Boyajian. Armenian-Egyptian man, fifties, soft-spoken, precise, polite and very shrewd.
text: Mr. Giza. I hear you sell to ladies in Garden City. I sell to dealers in Paris. Perhaps we can be useful to each other.

speaker: hagop
voice_brief: Hagop Boyajian. Armenian-Egyptian man, fifties, soft-spoken, precise, polite and very shrewd.
text: Anything, at a dealer's price. That is the local market here. I do not argue, I do not cry, I pay. When you need money more than margin, come to me.

speaker: hagop
voice_brief: Hagop Boyajian. Armenian-Egyptian man, fifties, soft-spoken, precise, polite and very shrewd.
text: The reverse. I have a client in Paris who wants a Kashan, a real one, midnight blue. Find one and I pay three hundred and twenty. Rashid had one. So did a widow near the Citadel.

speaker: hagop
voice_brief: Hagop Boyajian. Armenian-Egyptian man, fifties, soft-spoken, precise, polite and very shrewd.
text: Let me see. Kork wool... yes. That is a real Kashan. Three hundred and twenty, as promised, and my respect, which is worth more.

speaker: hagop
voice_brief: Hagop Boyajian. Armenian-Egyptian man, fifties, soft-spoken, precise, polite and very shrewd.
text: The telegraph boy? He is at the office by the Opera. Tell him Hagop says his mother is too generous.

speaker: sheikhomar
voice_brief: Sheikh Omar. Big-voiced festival organiser, cheerful, loud, blesses everything.
text: Welcome to Tanta, God bless you! If you come at the moulid you will sell everything you own, and your cat. The rest of the year we are farmers.

speaker: sheikhomar
voice_brief: Sheikh Omar. Big-voiced festival organiser, cheerful, loud, blesses everything.
text: Warm rugs for village houses, strong ones for tents. Nobody here wants silk. Silk is for Cairo people who have chairs.

speaker: pericles
voice_brief: Pericles Stavrou. Alexandrian Greek man, forties, elegant, fast, switches between charm and business.
text: Kyrie, a carpet man! Everyone in Alexandria is a cotton man or a shipping man. You will be lonely. Where are you sailing?

speaker: pericles
voice_brief: Pericles Stavrou. Alexandrian Greek man, forties, elegant, fast, switches between charm and business.
text: Jaffa in two days, Beirut in three, Istanbul in five if the sea is kind. Buy a passage from the harbour. Deck class is cheap and the view is free.

speaker: pericles
voice_brief: Pericles Stavrou. Alexandrian Greek man, forties, elegant, fast, switches between charm and business.
text: In twenty-two, when Smyrna burned, my cousins came here with nothing but the carpets they could carry. Many of those carpets are now on the floors of Egypt. If you have one with a star in the middle, it may have come on our ships.

speaker: pericles
voice_brief: Pericles Stavrou. Alexandrian Greek man, forties, elegant, fast, switches between charm and business.
text: Then you sold a piece of somebody's house. I hope you sold it to someone who deserved it.

speaker: pericles
voice_brief: Pericles Stavrou. Alexandrian Greek man, forties, elegant, fast, switches between charm and business.
text: The Ptolemy and the Corniche Palace buy hard-wearing rugs by the dozen. They pay well for dark colours that hide sand. The local market here reflects that.

speaker: captainreed
voice_brief: Captain Reed. Englishman, sixties, clipped naval voice, kindly, a bit deaf.
text: Carpets, eh? The liners stop here for six hours. Passengers want something "authentically Oriental" to prove they went east of Malta. They pay for a good yarn more than a good rug.

speaker: captainreed
voice_brief: Captain Reed. Englishman, sixties, clipped naval voice, kindly, a bit deaf.
text: Sells like ice. Mind you, some chap sold my wife a "Pharaoh's prayer mat" in 1911. Made in Manchester. I still have it. It is a very good mat.

speaker: anastasios
voice_brief: Brother Anastasios. Greek monk, seventies, very quiet, gentle, precise English with a Greek accent.
text: You have come a long way to sell carpets to monks. We do not buy. But we remember. What do you wish to know?

speaker: anastasios
voice_brief: Brother Anastasios. Greek monk, seventies, very quiet, gentle, precise English with a Greek accent.
text: Look at the back, not the front. Old wool is worn smooth by hands, not by brushes. Natural dyes change shade row by row. Chemical dyes are the same colour from end to end, like a lie told too well.

speaker: anastasios
voice_brief: Brother Anastasios. Greek monk, seventies, very quiet, gentle, precise English with a Greek accent.
text: The Tarabin. East of here, two days. They trade kilims for sugar and news. Bring news. They value it more than sugar.

speaker: salim
voice_brief: Salim ibn Eid. Young Bedouin man, calm, proud, dry wit, speaks slowly.
text: A townsman with a cat, in the desert. My father will want to hear about this. Sit. Coffee first, business later, perhaps never.

speaker: salim
voice_brief: Salim ibn Eid. Young Bedouin man, calm, proud, dry wit, speaks slowly.
text: The English have a new high commissioner and the price of sugar went up? Then nothing has changed. Thank you, it is still news. Our weavers will trade with you as friends.

speaker: salim
voice_brief: Salim ibn Eid. Young Bedouin man, calm, proud, dry wit, speaks slowly.
text: Safe for our friends. For others, there are young men with rifles and no sheep. If they stop you, say you ate with Salim ibn Eid.

speaker: abuyusef
voice_brief: Abu Yusef. Jaffa merchant, fifties, jovial, generous, loud laugh.
text: Egyptian! Take an orange. Take two. In Jaffa we pay for everything in oranges. Jerusalem is up the road, you want to go up, everybody goes up.

speaker: abuyusef
voice_brief: Abu Yusef. Jaffa merchant, fifties, jovial, generous, loud laugh.
text: Old things with papers. The consuls and the professors want to know who made it and when. Bring a good story and the paper to prove it.

speaker: boulos
voice_brief: Father Boulos. Armenian priest, sixties, warm baritone, speaks slowly and kindly.
text: Peace be with you. Most dealers who come to Jerusalem want to sell to pilgrims. What do you want?

speaker: boulos
voice_brief: Father Boulos. Armenian priest, sixties, warm baritone, speaks slowly and kindly.
text: Truth. A documented rug here is worth a third more than the same rug with a story. People come to Jerusalem looking for true things, even when they buy carpets.

speaker: nadia
voice_brief: Nadia Sursock. Beiruti woman, forties, sophisticated, amused, French-inflected Arabic.
text: Egypt sends me a carpet seller. How charming. Silk is my family's business, so do not tell me anything about silk I do not already know.

speaker: nadia
voice_brief: Nadia Sursock. Beiruti woman, forties, sophisticated, amused, French-inflected Arabic.
text: Half of what is sold as Damascus silk was woven in Kayseri for export. The other half was woven in Damascus for tourists. Only a real expert in the Hamidiyya can tell you which half you own.

speaker: nadia
voice_brief: Nadia Sursock. Beiruti woman, forties, sophisticated, amused, French-inflected Arabic.
text: Farid al-Khatib. He is rude, slow and always right. Over the mountains, a day and a half.

speaker: farid
voice_brief: Farid al-Khatib. Old Damascene expert, seventies, slow, severe, few words, occasional dry kindness.
text: Rashid's boy. Your father owed me an opinion and never came to collect it. Show me what you have. Do not tell me what it is. Tell me nothing.

speaker: farid
voice_brief: Farid al-Khatib. Old Damascene expert, seventies, slow, severe, few words, occasional dry kindness.
text: I turn it over. I count. I smell it. Then I listen to the dealer lie, and I measure the lie against the rug. The rug is usually more honest.

speaker: farid
voice_brief: Farid al-Khatib. Old Damascene expert, seventies, slow, severe, few words, occasional dry kindness.
text: Hm.

speaker: kevork
voice_brief: Kevork Tashjian. Aleppo Armenian, fifties, energetic, bargains while he talks.
text: You came from Egypt to Aleppo to buy Anatolian rugs? Smart. Here they are half what they are in Cairo. Take ten. Take twenty.

speaker: kevork
voice_brief: Kevork Tashjian. Aleppo Armenian, fifties, energetic, bargains while he talks.
text: Konya, Kayseri, the villages in between. Go to Konya and they are cheaper still, but you ride two weeks and pay the Turkish customs. For you, Aleppo is enough.

speaker: ayse
voice_brief: Ayşe Hanım. Anatolian woman, fifties, practical, kind, speaks Turkish-accented Arabic.
text: An Egyptian in Konya! The star rugs you sell in Giza, we make here. My sister wove the one with the caravan star. Maybe you sold it.

speaker: ayse
voice_brief: Ayşe Hanım. Anatolian woman, fifties, practical, kind, speaks Turkish-accented Arabic.
text: Then my sister will be pleased. Tell your lady the star means a place to rest. Buy from us and I will give you the good ones.

speaker: selim
voice_brief: Selim Bey. Ottoman gentleman, sixties, formal, melancholy, very polite Istanbul Turkish accent.
text: The palace carpets? Some are in museums now, some are in my cellar, and some are on the floors of men who do not deserve them. What kind of man are you?

speaker: selim
voice_brief: Selim Bey. Ottoman gentleman, sixties, formal, melancholy, very polite Istanbul Turkish accent.
text: A good answer. Come back when you have a house to sell from, not a corner. Then we will talk seriously.

speaker: haji
voice_brief: Haji Karim. Persian merchant, sixties, poetic, unhurried, Persian-accented Arabic.
text: You crossed the desert for carpets? The carpets cross it for you, if you wait. But since you are here, I will show you Kashans at a Baghdad price.

speaker: rashid
voice_brief: Uncle Rashid. Old Cairo merchant, sixties, gruff, teasing, secretly fond, fast talker.
text: Go to Alexandria. Walk the Souq el-Attarin, or find its dealers on the Market tab. Choose one rug with your own eyes and pay for it — the seller will send Rashid the receipt, and that is proof enough.

speaker: rashid

direction: Mission "Rashid's errand in Alexandria": errand done.

speaker: rashid
voice_brief: Uncle Rashid. Old Cairo merchant, sixties, gruff, teasing, secretly fond, fast talker.
text: A merchant who carries everything on his own back is a porter, not a merchant. Buy two donkeys or camels, go to Tanta, bring my bale. Keep two rugs for your trouble.
direction: Mission "Beasts of burden": handing over the errand.

speaker: rashid
voice_brief: Uncle Rashid. Old Cairo merchant, sixties, gruff, teasing, secretly fond, fast talker.
text: You look almost like a merchant now. Almost. The donkey looks more like one than you.

speaker: rashid
voice_brief: Uncle Rashid. Old Cairo merchant, sixties, gruff, teasing, secretly fond, fast talker.
text: Farid al-Khatib in Damascus knows every loom from Aleppo to Kayseri. Take it to him. Pack it for the road. And do not let him see you are nervous.
direction: Mission "Your father's rug": handing over the errand.

speaker: abuhamid

text: His cousins are waiting on the Suez road for your next caravan. Do not go alone. Hire men who have fought before, and show them your caravan is not worth the trouble.
direction: Mission "Selim's cousins": handing over the errand.

speaker: malek
text: Sit anywhere. The stools are all equally bad.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: You are new. Everyone is new once. Then they complain.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Welcome. That is the last nice thing I say today, so remember it.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: I am Malek, Al-Mallem. The boss. And there is nobody else here to be boss of.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Beans are on. The grill is not. Do not ask me about the grill before eleven.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Early. Good. The early ones complain less; they are still asleep.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Morning. The ful is hot and the bread is yesterday's. Today's bread is late. Bread is always late.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: I light the charcoal before the sun. I put the beans on.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Now what?
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: And by noon everyone wants lunch at the same time. Nobody thinks of me.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Sit, sit. If the stool wobbles, that is the stool.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: The grill is hot, the meat is honest, and I am tired. Two out of three is good for Giza.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Late. The grill is going cold. So am I.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Evening. If you wanted kebab, you should have wanted it at noon.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Bah. A customer at the end of the day. Good. The coins were lonely.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Sit. I am counting. If you talk, I lose count, and then I start again, and then I am angry.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: You again. The food has not changed. Neither have I.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Your stool is free. Nobody else wants it either.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Back for more. I knew it. Nobody listens to me, but they come back.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: If you come every day, people will think the food is good. Do not ruin my name.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Ha. Alive. I said you would get lost. I was nearly right.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Where were you? Never mind. Everywhere is worse than here; you know that now.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: You look like someone who ate road bread for a week. Sit down before you fall down.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: You look terrible. That is not an insult; it is a diagnosis. Tea.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Sit before you fall on my tables. They are older than you and weaker.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Tired? Eat something with meat in it, then go to bed. Two pieces of advice, both free, both ignored.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: I can hear your stomach from the grill. Order something before it frightens the customers.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: You are hungry. Do not argue; I have seen hungry before. It looks exactly like you.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Sit. Eat. Then talk. In that order, or not at all.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Your rug is under the tables. A man spilled stew on it this morning. It survived. I am almost impressed.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Look at the floor. Your rug. Grease, boots, tea, one cat. Still alive. Hm.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Customers ask where I bought the rug. I tell them a thief sold it to me. They laugh. I do not.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: I came to your stall. Everything was too pretty. Pretty does not last here.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Your rugs looked at me like they were too good for my floor. They were right. That is the problem.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: It is all on the board. Read it slowly; it does not get cheaper if you read it fast.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Kofta, kebab, liver. The pot is whatever the pot is today.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Ha. You want to see the menu. It is four things and some bread.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: The board does not lie. I wrote it. I do not lie either; I only complain.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Kofta is good. Kebab is better and costs more. That is how the world works; do not look surprised.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: You want it cheaper? I can put the meat back on the sheep.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Kofta. Mince, onion, fire. Nothing clever. Clever food is for hotels.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: My father's kofta. He also complained the whole time he made it, so it is authentic.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Is the kofta good? Of course it is good. I make it with my own hands.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Straight off the charcoal. Burn your mouth if you like; I do not give refunds for patience.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Eat it hot. Cold kebab is just an argument.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Liver. Hot, fast, honest. Like an argument with my supplier.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Lamb. I had four this morning. Now I have fewer. Life is like that.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Beans. The cheapest thing in Giza that is not advice.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Soup. It fills you up and it does not argue.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Ful. Cheap, filling, and it will still be with you at sunset.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: It lasts longer than my patience. Take water.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Salted beef. You will want water before Suez. You will want water before the end of the street.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Wrapped twice. If it goes off, that is the road, not me.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Bastirma from Cairo. My supplier swears by it. He swears by everything. Take water.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: For the road? Eat it slowly. The desert is long and my patience is short; one of them will run out.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Tea. One glass. Two glasses and you will start talking to me.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Sugar is extra. No, it is not. Bah. Drink it.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Tea. The only thing in this shop that is never late.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: On my account. Do not get used to it. I already regret it.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Free. Because of the rug. If the rug dies, you pay double.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Eat. It is paid for. By me. Ha. Do not tell the bean man.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Ha. The sheep has finished its shift.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Gone. Come earlier. Everyone who comes late says they will come earlier.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Finished. Everything good finishes early. Remember that about life.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Coins again. Funny how they never breed overnight.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: The grill is cold. I can sell you a parcel. I cannot sell you a fire.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: The fire is out. The coins are counted. They were wrong again. They are always wrong.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: The fire is out. Fire does not come back because you are hungry.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Cold grill. Parcels, tea, soup. Or tomorrow. Tomorrow is very popular.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: You are full. I can see it from here. Eat it anyway; I already cooked it.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Another plate? You will roll home. I will not carry you.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: You have the money or you have the story. I take the money.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Bah. Come back when your purse agrees with your stomach.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Count your coins. I counted mine. Neither of us is happy.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Go. Come back hungry.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Mind the step. Everyone trips on the step. I will not fix it.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Close the door. No, leave it, it is too hot. Halfway. Go.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: I work alone. Partners eat the profits and then they eat the kofta.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: One grill, four tables, one owner. If I had two grills I would need two of me. One of me is enough trouble.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: The tourists ask if it is authentic. I tell them it is lunch.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: The charcoal man comes on Tuesdays. Some Tuesdays. He thinks the week is a suggestion.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Al-Mallem means the boss. Everyone calls me that. Even the sheep, I think.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Boo Rayan, because of my son. He is at school learning to argue. He is already better at it than me.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Malek. It means "the owner". I own four tables, one grill and no patience. Sit.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: The storeroom? Charcoal, onions, sacks. Nothing else. Why do you ask? Do not ask.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Do not go in the back. It is not dangerous. It is private. There is a difference, mostly.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: You heard something in the back? That was the onions. They settle.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: I keep the good bastirma in the back. Also other things. Eat your food.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: The Englishman with the bottles smells rugs for money. Arran. He eats here and asks what is in the kofta. Meat. It is meat.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Rashid sells you rugs on credit? Brave man. Or stupid. In Giza those are cousins.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Coffee house tells more stories than the newspaper and half as many lies. Do not quote me.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: The bean man across the lane says his ful is better. His ful is wet. I said nothing. I am saying it now.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Going on the road? Take parcels. Take water. Salted meat makes you thirsty; I say it every time and every time they come back dry.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: My parcels keep a week. Less in the summer. If it smells wrong, it is wrong; throw it away.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Eat before you sell. A hungry seller gives discounts. A fed seller argues. I argue.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: In khamsin season wrap your face and your bread. Sand gets into both.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Yes, he lives in the back. No, he does not have a name. He has an appetite.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: He is not a pet. He is staff. Staff eat. Staff do not take orders, which makes him like every other staff.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Nabil al-Khatib has not come back. The kebab price has not come down. Both good.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Do not feed him. I feed him. If two people feed him, he expects it of everyone.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Arthur brings animals out from London for the zoo. Once he brought one more than the paperwork. Now it lives with me. Ha.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Arthur eats here when a ship comes in. He pays. He is the only Englishman who pays without asking what is in it.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Arthur says the zoo has a proper house for him. He also says the zoo has rules. My storeroom has kebab. You see the problem.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: I need a rug for under the tables. Dark, thick, forgiving. I will come to your stall and look. Do not expect me to like anything.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Show me ugly and strong and I will pay. Show me pretty and I will laugh.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Grease, boots, tea. That is what the rug must survive. Also my customers. Mostly my customers.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Your rug is still alive. Grease, boots, stew. Still alive.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: If it lasts the winter, I want another by the door. Do not start counting the money.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: People sit longer since the rug. Longer is bad; they order tea and stay all afternoon. Hm. It is a good rug.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Hm. That is the price. I am not sure it is the rug. Keep it. Maybe I come back.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Fine, the number is fine. My stomach says no. I listen to my stomach; it has never lost me money.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: Ha. You almost had me. Almost is not a sale. I will think about it.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.

speaker: malek
text: I need to look at my floor again. Do not sell it to the first fool who asks. Unless he pays more. Bah.
direction: In his shop: blunt, warm underneath, dry.
